scenes.title: The Nine Clocks
paragraphs: *Command deck, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 06:10*
Nine clocks hung on the forward bulkhead, and no two of them agreed.

The Kerrel Assembly kept them there on purpose, one for each inhabited system that still sent timing, so that its officers could see at a glance how far the sky had come apart. The spread was four minutes now. Yesterday it had been ninety seconds. Beyond the viewport the stars of the Hesper cluster sat a hair out of place, as though someone had jogged the table they stood on.
Commander Maren Vask met Illuminara at the lock with a slate in each hand and no greeting.

**Maren Vask**  
You have until ten-forty tomorrow morning. That is not my deadline. It belongs to the Triple Key. Kerrel, the Ussu Chorus and the Halcyon fleet each hold a third of a strike order, and all three keys are turned to ready. At ten-forty the thing in the outer reach is hit with everything the Reach owns.

**Wren Odira**  
It has not fired on anyone. I would like that said before anybody says invader.
Wren had come aboard ahead of her, as she always did, and was already doing what she did best, which was standing beside the loudest clock.

**Maren Vask**  
It has taken the tide-songs from two Ussu brood-worlds. It cost a convoy its navigation for six hours. It is a body the size of a small moon, nobody can find its edge, and the sky bends where it sits. I do not need it to fire, Wren. I need it to stop.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will ask what you would ask. What is it doing, in order, and when? Not what it means. The log.

Vask gave her the left-hand slate. Nine entries. Each was a pulse: the stars within a light-year swung a few arcseconds off their places, hung there for about forty minutes, and swung back. Illuminara let AC show her the lines of strain across the cluster, the way a map shows slope, and the strain agreed with the log. A long swell, then release, then a flat quiet.
She did not look at the swells. She looked at the gaps between them.

**Illuminara**  
Twelve hours. Ten and a half. Nine and a bit. Each gap is seven-eighths of the one before it.

**Maren Vask**  
A decaying signal. Alarms do that. So does a fuse.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. A series that shrinks by a fixed fraction has a sum, and the sum is a date. The last gap was four hours forty-three. Seven times that is thirty-three hours. At about one tomorrow afternoon the gaps become shorter than the pulses themselves, and the pulses run together into one. Your Key turns two hours and twenty minutes before that.
Nobody on the deck said anything. One of the nine clocks ticked over, three seconds ahead of its neighbour.

**Illuminara**  
It is an ending or a beginning. I do not know which, and neither do you. Before anything else I want a way of finding out that none of us has to take on faith.

scenes.title: Seven-Eighths
paragraphs: *Operations hall, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 07:40*

The delegates came by relay: three faces and one absence. Commander Vask for Kerrel. Iyo-Seven for the Ussu Chorus, who was seven bodies in a tide-tank and spoke by turns. Tally for the Halcyon fleet, a point of cold light on the table that answered in the flat, courteous voice of a machine that had decided long ago not to be liked.
Illuminara set two stories side by side and asked them to distrust both equally.

**Illuminara**  
Story one. A being from outside our cosmos is in labour. The pulses are contractions, and the gaps shorten because that is what labour does. Between pulses the strain falls back to the same floor, because between contractions a body rests. Story two. This is an incursion wearing a mother's shape. The pulses are a charge, and the gaps shorten because the weapon is nearly ready. Between pulses the floor would climb, because a thing that is charging does not rest.

**Maren Vask**  
Story two is the one a mother's story is built to hide.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. That is why I am not asking you to believe either. I am asking you to predict. Each of you measures the pulses with your own instruments and writes down when the next one begins and how high the floor sits after it. Seal it. Nobody opens anybody's envelope until the pulse has come.

**Tally**  
Kerrel keeps time by atoms, the Chorus by song, my fleet by ranging pulsars. Our errors are unrelated. If all three of us land together, it will not be because we copied one another.

**Iyo-Seven**  
We add what the Commander has not said. Each pulse unmakes the songs of our young. We do not ask for pity. We ask that your test be quick.

The tenth pulse began at 08:07 and held the sky for forty minutes. Tally had sealed 08:06. The Chorus had sealed 08:09, Kerrel 08:05. Behind the swell the floor dropped back to exactly where it had dropped before, within the width of a pencil line.

**Maren Vask**  
Once. A coin can land once.

**Illuminara**  
A coin can. So we spend every pulse we have as another throw, and we write down now what would make us stop. If the floor rises more than three parts in a hundred of the peak, or a gap breaks the seven-eighths by more than a quarter of itself, the story is false and the Key turns. We write that while none of us is frightened. We will not be able to write it when we are.
Tally took the line and logged it without comment. After a moment so did Iyo-Seven, seven bodies nodding out of step. Vask took longest.

**Maren Vask**  
And while the coin is still in the air, you intend to go and ask the thing itself.

**Illuminara**  
I intend to ask her what no instrument of yours can read.

**Wren Odira**  
I'll keep the clock. I say your name at every hour. You answer, or I come in.

**Illuminara**  
You can't come into a window.

**Wren Odira**  
Watch me find out.

scenes.title: The Window
paragraphs: *Tide-boat Long Patience, outer reach · Day one, 09:20*

The Long Patience hung a light-year and a half from the guest, which was as near as the Ussu would take her. Distance did not help. Illuminara felt the thing out in the dark as a slow tilt in the floor of everything, a hill her body leaned away from.

She made the window the way she had made them before: a place where one consciousness could meet another without either being crushed, wide enough that the guest's size could not spill into her. The guest came into it as a long dim shoreline, warm at the far end, with something at the warm end turning over in its sleep.

**Anomei**  
You are small, and not afraid enough. Good. The others sent engines.

**Illuminara**  
I am Illuminara. Are you hurting my cluster on purpose?

**Anomei**  
I am hurting it by being. You are a room, and I was offered a closet. At the first door they closed a gate. At the second they sang me away. At the third they sent a fleet. I did not come for your stars. I came for what I carry.

**Illuminara**  
Tell me what you carry.

**Anomei**  
A child. In your word, which is a poor word for it: soon.
The shoreline shivered. Out in the cluster, a swell began to build.

**Anomei**  
I will tell you what I have told no one, because you asked and did not aim. If I am refused a place, I will bear the child where I stand. Its first breath will make a sphere of my home's law three light-years wide, and everything inside will become part of that law. It will not be malice. It will be a birth. I would do it, small one. I would rather be the thing you fear than watch my child die in a closet.
Illuminara did not soften it. She had learned long ago that the worst thing to do with a true threat was to make it smaller for the people who had to decide about it.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will carry that sentence to three suspicious powers exactly as you said it. They need to know what refusing you costs. And they will believe the rest of what you tell them only if you have hidden nothing.

**Anomei**  
You will turn them against me.

**Illuminara**  
Perhaps. Or they will find that you did not lie when lying would have helped you. Now. What must the room be? Do not say large. Tell me how.

Anomei had no measure for it in any language Illuminara could translate. But the swell was still rising, and Illuminara understood that she had been standing in the answer for three days. Each pulse was the child leaning on the walls of the room, and the lean grew by exactly as much as the wall was missing. She ran the peak through the strain map and the map drew a sphere around the guest: six-tenths of a light-year, growing to a little under one at the end.
Then she searched the charts she carried for a place that was empty to that radius and had stayed empty.

**Illuminara**  
There is a void at the cluster's edge. Dornrath. Nothing in it larger than a comet for nearly two light-years in every direction.

**Anomei**  
At the second door they spoke of it. They called it the ocean of nobody.

**Illuminara**  
It is not nobody's. Nine thousand people live on its rim, in the dark, on purpose. Asking them is the first thing I must do, and they can say no.
The shoreline went quiet for a long moment.

**Anomei**  
Then you will ask them honestly, and I will have to wait for an answer from strangers about my child. I have never asked a stranger for anything.

**Wren Odira**  
Illuminara.

**Illuminara**  
Here, Wren. Hour one. Here.

scenes.title: The Ocean of Nobody
paragraphs: *The Quiet Rung, rim of the Dornrath void · Day one, 12:15*

The Tenders lived in the dark because they had wanted quiet, and three generations had not talked them out of it. Nine thousand people on a ring of habitats lit by ice-farm glow; nothing but the far cold stars over the glass. Halcyon's probes had gone through the void in four hours and Tally read out the survey as flatly as a ledger: empty to 1.9 light-years from the centre, one dead comet, no traffic, no dust worth the name.
Elder Pell Auro heard it standing, one hand on the rail of her council balcony.

**Pell Auro**  
So you have come to rent our dark.

**Illuminara**  
I have come to ask for it. I cannot rent what is not mine, and you may refuse.

**Pell Auro**  
And if I do?

**Illuminara**  
Then I go back to a table where three keys are turning and tell them to find another room. There is no other room. I will not pretend that costs you nothing to be asked.
Pell asked to see the pulses herself, and Tally threw the floor trace on the wall: the swells rising, the floor underneath staying flat as a table. Pell looked at it for a long time.

**Pell Auro**  
I have borne four children. The floor goes flat. Between, you rest. You have to.

**Tally**  
A Tender's testimony cannot be entered as a measurement.

**Pell Auro**  
No. I am not a measurement. I am the owner.

Illuminara let that stand, because it was true, and because the Halcyon machine had just made the better argument for her without meaning to: whatever Pell believed, she was reading the same instruments as everyone else.

**Illuminara**  
There is a risk and I would rather say it than have you find it. I got the size of the room from the lean of the pulses. If I am wrong by a factor of two, the edge of her sphere meets your rim.

**Pell Auro**  
Then you are asking nine thousand people to stake their lives on your arithmetic.

**Illuminara**  
I am asking you to check it. Have your own people do the sum. And hear the rest, which is that nothing so far tells us whether this is a mother or a weapon. Only the end of the series can. So the plan has to be one we would carry out even if the worse story is true.

She laid it out for the Elder and, by relay, for Vask and Iyo-Seven. The guest would come to Dornrath in five hops, each made only in the rest between pulses, while she was folded small and could do nothing but travel. The three fleets would hold at three light-years with the Key still turned. The cancel conditions were already sealed. If the story broke, they would strike a mother or a weapon in the middle of an empty ocean, with nothing of theirs and nothing of the Tenders' within the reach of what she could do.

**Pell Auro**  
The inner ring. Eight hundred of us live nearest the void. They go to your Kerrel transports for the day, with their children and their animals.

**Maren Vask**  
Done.

**Pell Auro**  
And afterward, whatever the sphere leaves in my sky, we sit at the table when it is decided what happens to it. Not as witnesses. As a hand.

**Illuminara**  
As a hand.
The Elder looked a moment longer at the flat line on the wall.

**Pell Auro**  
Tell her the dark is lent. Not given.

**Illuminara**  
I will tell her exactly that.

scenes.title: Five Windows
paragraphs: *The outer lanes · Day one, 15:33 to Day two, 01:30*

The first hop opened at 15:33, the instant the twelfth pulse released the sky. The guest folded small, and for forty-four minutes the Ussu tide-boats sang a line of steady space from the outer reach toward Dornrath, and the thing that could bend the stars crossed two light-years without bending anything. Tally's probes ranged her the whole way. Vask's ships hung at the edges with their guns trained, and the guest had asked for them to be trained, so that no one could say she had come unwatched.

The second hop and the third passed the same way. At each pulse the three sealed predictions came in within a few minutes of each other and within a few minutes of the pulse. The floor stayed flat. Nobody called it proof. But Illuminara noticed, from the tide-boat, that the officers on the Anchor's deck had stopped saying story two.
The fourth pulse came eleven minutes early.
It came at 21:56 where all three predictions had said 22:07, and the sky tilted and held. On the Anchor's deck Vask's hand went to the Key before the thought did.

**Maren Vask**  
It is early. It broke the series.

**Tally**  
It broke it by nine per cent of a gap. The sealed limit is a quarter. The floor is flat.

**Maren Vask**  
Say it is not your guess, Illuminara.

**Illuminara**  
It is not my guess. It is in the tolerance we wrote down this morning, when nobody was frightened. I wrote it for exactly this minute. Please hold your hand where it is.

The hand stayed. The cost was real. The early pulse had shifted the whole series, and three instruments refit it on the spot. The last window, the one between the sixteenth and seventeenth pulses, shrank from fifty-seven minutes to forty-three. Anomei needed forty-nine to cross the final two light-years folded small. A flinch at either end would drop her into the sky of the Reach at full size, with the contractions less than an hour apart.

**Anomei**  
I cannot do it faster.

**Iyo-Seven**  
The Chorus can.
Seven bodies in a tide-tank, singing as one for the first time in Illuminara's hearing.

**Iyo-Seven**  
We cannot move her. That is hers. But we can hold the strain steady along the last line so she need not bend around it. It will cost us the songs of two more broods. We choose it.

**Anomei**  
Why?

**Iyo-Seven**  
Because we have lost songs to your pulses for three days, and not one of them has come at the same hour as the last. They come as a body that is trying not to hurt us. We have felt it. We know the difference between an engine and a creature that is trying.

The fifth hop opened at 00:42. It took forty-one minutes. At 01:23 the guest unfolded at the heart of the Dornrath void with two minutes to spare, and the sky of the Reach, for the first time in four days, did not tilt.

scenes.title: The Cradle
paragraphs: *Dornrath void, the Quiet Rung · Day two, 12:20*

The last hours of the series were not measured in minutes. By noon the pulses had run together into one long swell with no floor beneath it, which the Key's cancel conditions did not forbid, because the sealed text said the floor would vanish when the gaps did. Eight hundred Tenders slept in Kerrel transports three light-years away. The three fleets held their positions at the edge of the void, as promised, with their keys turned. Wren sat in the lock of the last tide-boat with a Halcyon clock on one knee and a Kerrel clock on the other, and for the first time she did not say Illuminara's name every hour. She said it every ten minutes.

**Wren Odira**  
Illuminara.

**Illuminara**  
Here.

Inside the window the shoreline had become something Illuminara had no word for, a warmth the size of a world with a sharp, small pain at its centre. She did not do the birth. It was not hers. She did what a window was for: she held a place where Anomei could be as large as her labour needed and not be afraid of the size of it, and where the small one at the centre of that place could go on being small.

**Anomei**  
I am afraid.

**Illuminara**  
I know. Afraid is allowed. I am here.

**Anomei**  
If it goes wrong, say that you tried to tell them it was a mother.

**Illuminara**  
If it goes wrong, I will say that you told me the truth when it cost you. I will say that first.
The three sealed predictions of the end of the series came in at 12:41, 12:58 and 13:11. The swell ended at 12:58.

The child's first breath made a sphere of its home's law, and the sphere was nine-tenths of a light-year across at the edge. Tally measured it within a hair of Illuminara's number. It lay in the middle of the void with its edge a long way from the Rung, a warm bright pearl in the dark, and the strain on every star in the cluster let go at once like a held breath.
On Wren's knees, the Kerrel clock and the Halcyon clock, which had refused to agree for four days, ticked over together.
In the Anchor's command deck the nine clocks on the bulkhead were within a second of one another before Vask had finished turning her key back.

The Cradle Accord was settled by the end of the day, in the window, with the Elder, the Commander, Iyo-Seven and Tally all speaking to a mother who held her child in a sphere that nobody else could enter. The terms were exact, because the powers would not accept anything vaguer, and Illuminara, who had spent days making them say what would change their minds, did not ask them to. The sphere's edge would shrink as the child's body learned the law of this cosmos; Tally projected forty years before it dropped below the threshold at which the two could leave. Until then the Tenders would host them, the three powers would keep their instruments on the void, and the Tenders would hold a hand at every table. Messages could pass to the child's family through a single beacon, read by all four parties. No body could cross without the unanimous consent of all four.

**Anomei**  
You have put my family's door in four hands.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. I cannot promise any of them will turn it. I can tell you they chose to hold it, and that at the other three doors there was no hand to turn.

Anomei was silent for a long time. Then the shoreline softened, and what came into the window was not an answer but a name, which Illuminara translated as best she could. It meant something close to Hold.

Afterward, on the rim, Wren found her standing at the glass. Beyond it the dark was no longer dark; it had a small pearl in the middle of it, which would be there for forty years. The Tenders had lost their sky, and the Chorus had lost the songs of four broods that would not return. The powers would not forget the fear. None of that was small.

**Wren Odira**  
You didn't make them trust her.

**Illuminara**  
No. I made it so they didn't have to.

**Wren Odira**  
Come and drink something hot.
Illuminara went.

scenes.title: Five Windows
paragraphs: *The outer lanes · Day one, 15:33 to Day two, 01:30*

The first hop opened at 15:33, the instant the twelfth pulse released the sky. Vask's ships hung at the edges with their guns trained, as the guest herself had asked, so that no one could say she had come unwatched. After each pulse Corin sent his projection to all four envelopes: nought point nine eight, nought point nine seven, nought point nine eight. The floor stayed flat. Nobody called it proof, but the officers on the Anchor's deck had stopped saying story two.
The fourth pulse came eleven minutes early.
It came at 21:56 where all three predictions had said 22:07, and the sky tilted and held. On the Anchor's deck Vask's hand went to the Key before the thought did.

**Maren Vask**

**Tally**  
By nine per cent of a gap. The sealed limit is a quarter. The floor is flat.

The hand stayed. That crisis was over, and had been paid for in advance. The other one was not.

**Anomei**  
I cannot do it faster.

**Maren Vask**

Seven bodies in a tide-tank began to sing as one, for the first time in Illuminara's hearing.

**Iyo-Seven**

**Maren Vask**

**Iyo-Seven**

scenes.title: The Cradle
paragraphs: *Dornrath void, the Quiet Rung · Day two, 12:20*

By noon the pulses had run together into one long swell with no floor beneath it, which the Key's cancel conditions did not forbid, because the sealed text said the floor would vanish when the gaps did. Eight hundred Tenders slept in Kerrel transports three light-years away. The three fleets held their positions at the edge of the void, as promised, with their keys turned. Wren sat in the lock of the last tide-boat with a Halcyon clock on one knee and a Kerrel clock on the other, and for the first time she did not say Illuminara's name every hour. She said it every ten minutes.

**Wren Odira**  
Illuminara.

**Illuminara**  
Here.

Inside the window the shoreline had become a warmth the size of a world with a sharp, small pain at its centre. Illuminara did not do the birth. It was not hers. She held a place where Anomei could be as large as her labour needed and not be afraid of it, and where the small one at the centre could go on being small.
Then the pain sharpened, and Anomei, who had never asked a stranger for anything, did what a body does in that pain. She reached outward.

On the Rung, Corin's projection went past one point two. Tally said so, flat as a ledger. At that radius the fringe of the law touched the glass where eight thousand Tenders were still asleep in their own beds.

**Anomei**  
I cannot hold it in. It is going out of me.

**Illuminara**  
Then do not hold it. Lean on me.

**Anomei**

**Illuminara**

She had stood three days in the answer. Now she stepped into it. The hill she had always leaned away from came down on her, and she widened the window to take its weight. It was the first thing in the whole story that nobody had asked her to do and nobody else could have done.

Illuminara.

**Wren Odira**  
Illuminara.

**Illuminara**  
Here.

**Illuminara**

**Anomei**

**Illuminara**  
No. I made it so they didn't have to.

story.title: The Guest Too Large for the Universe
story.deck: A visitor from outside the cosmos is bending the stars of the Hesper cluster, three armed powers are turning their keys, and Illuminara has to find out whether what looks like an attack is a birth, in a way none of them has to take on trust.
story.shape: A convergent clock; each scene turns a claim into a prediction until four suspicious hands can read the answer on their own instruments.

scenes.title: The Nine Clocks
paragraphs: *Command deck, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 06:10*
Nine clocks hung on the forward bulkhead, and no two of them agreed.

The Kerrel Assembly kept them there on purpose, one for each inhabited system that still sent timing, so that its officers could see how far the sky had come apart. The spread was four minutes now. Yesterday it had been ninety seconds. Beyond the viewport the stars of the Hesper cluster sat a hair out of place, as though someone had jogged the table they stood on.
Commander Maren Vask met Illuminara at the lock with a slate in each hand and no greeting.

**Maren Vask**  
You have until ten-forty tomorrow morning. That is the Triple Key's deadline, not mine. Kerrel, the Ussu Chorus and the Halcyon fleet each hold a third of a strike order, and all three keys are turned to ready. At ten-forty the thing in the outer reach is hit with everything the Reach owns.

**Wren Odira**  
It has not fired on anyone. I would like that said before anybody says invader.

**Maren Vask**  
It has taken the tide-songs from two Ussu brood-worlds. It cost a convoy its navigation for six hours. It is a body the size of a small moon, and the sky bends where it sits. I do not need it to fire, Wren. I need it to stop.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will ask what you would ask. What is it doing, in order, and when? Not what it means. The log.

Nine entries. Each was a pulse: the stars within a light-year swung a few arcseconds off their places, hung there for about forty minutes, and swung back. Illuminara did not look at the swells. She looked at the gaps between them.

**Illuminara**  
Twelve hours. Ten and a half. Nine and a bit. Each gap is seven-eighths of the one before it.

**Maren Vask**  
A decaying signal. Alarms do that. So does a fuse.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. And a fuse has an end. The last gap was four hours forty-three, and seven times that is thirty-three hours. At about one tomorrow afternoon the gaps are shorter than the pulses, and the pulses run together into one. Your Key turns two hours and twenty minutes before that.
Nobody on the deck said anything. One of the nine clocks ticked over, three seconds ahead of its neighbour.

**Illuminara**  
It is an ending or a beginning. I do not know which, and neither do you. Before anything else I want a way of finding out that none of us has to take on faith.

scenes.title: Seven-Eighths
paragraphs: *Operations hall, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 07:40*

The delegates came by relay. Commander Vask for Kerrel. Iyo-Seven for the Ussu Chorus, seven bodies in a tide-tank who spoke by turns. Tally for the Halcyon fleet, a point of cold light on the table that answered in the flat, courteous voice of a machine that had decided long ago not to be liked.
Illuminara set two stories side by side and asked them to distrust both equally.

**Illuminara**

**Maren Vask**  
Story two is the one a mother's story is built to hide.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. So I am not asking you to believe either. I am asking you to predict. Each of you measures the pulses with your own instruments and seals when the next one begins and how high the floor sits after it. Nobody opens an envelope until the pulse has come.

**Iyo-Seven**

The tenth pulse began at 08:07 and held the sky for forty minutes. Tally had sealed 08:06, the Chorus 08:09, Kerrel 08:05. Behind the swell the floor dropped back to where it had dropped before, within the width of a pencil line.

**Maren Vask**  
Once. A coin can land once.

**Illuminara**

We write that while none of us is frightened. We will not be able to write it when we are.
Tally logged the line without comment. After a moment so did Iyo-Seven, seven bodies nodding out of step. Vask took longest.

**Maren Vask**  
And while the coin is in the air, you intend to go and ask the thing itself.

**Illuminara**  
I intend to ask it what no instrument of yours can read.

**Wren Odira**  
I keep the clock. I say your name every hour. You answer, or I come in.

**Illuminara**  
You can't come into a window.

**Wren Odira**  
Watch me find out.

scenes.title: The Window
paragraphs: *Tide-boat Long Patience, outer reach · Day one, 09:20*

The Long Patience hung a light-year and a half from the guest, as near as the Ussu would take her. Illuminara felt the thing out in the dark as a slow tilt in the floor of everything, a hill her body leaned away from.

You are small, and not afraid enough. Good. The others sent engines.

**Illuminara**  
I am Illuminara. Are you hurting my cluster on purpose?

**Anomei**

**Illuminara**  
Tell me what you carry.

**Anomei**  
A child. In your word, which is a poor word for it: soon.

**Anomei**

**Illuminara**  
It is not nobody's. Nine thousand people live on its rim, in the dark, on purpose. Asking them is the first thing I must do, and they can say no.

**Anomei**  
Then I must wait for an answer from strangers about my child. I have never asked a stranger for anything.

**Wren Odira**  
Illuminara.

**Illuminara**  
Here, Wren. Hour one. Here.

**Maren Vask**  
The Key has a deadline. Ten-forty.

**Illuminara**

**Maren Vask**  
Then it waits on your conditions. The moment one breaks, it turns. There will be no second warning.

**Pell Auro**

Illuminara.

**Wren Odira**  
Illuminara.

Here.

**Anomei**

**Anomei**

**Illuminara**  
No. I made it so they didn't have to.

**Wren Odira**  
Come and drink something hot.

story.title: The Guest Too Large for the Universe
story.deck: A visitor from outside the cosmos is bending the stars of the Hesper cluster, three armed powers are turning their keys, and Illuminara has to find out whether what looks like an attack is a birth, in a way none of them has to take on trust.
story.shape: A convergent clock; each scene turns a claim into a prediction until four suspicious hands can read the answer on their own instruments.

scenes.title: The Nine Clocks
paragraphs: *Command deck, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 06:10*
Nine clocks hung on the forward bulkhead, and no two of them agreed.

The Kerrel Assembly kept them there on purpose, one for each inhabited system that still sent timing, so that its officers could see how far the sky had come apart. The spread was four minutes now. Yesterday it had been ninety seconds. Beyond the viewport the stars of the Hesper cluster sat a hair out of place, as though someone had jogged the table they stood on.
Commander Maren Vask met Illuminara at the lock with a slate in each hand and no greeting.

**Maren Vask**  
You have until ten-forty tomorrow morning. That is the Triple Key's deadline, not mine. Kerrel, the Ussu Chorus and the Halcyon fleet each hold a third of a strike order, and all three keys are turned to ready. At ten-forty the thing in the outer reach is hit with everything the Reach owns.

**Wren Odira**  
It has not fired on anyone. I would like that said before anybody says invader.

**Maren Vask**  
It has taken the tide-songs from two Ussu brood-worlds. It cost a convoy its navigation for six hours. It is a body the size of a small moon, and the sky bends where it sits. I do not need it to fire, Wren. I need it to stop.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will ask what you would ask. What is it doing, in order, and when? Not what it means. The log.

Nine entries. Each was a pulse: the stars within a light-year swung a few arcseconds off their places, hung there for about forty minutes, and swung back. Illuminara did not look at the swells. She looked at the gaps between them.

**Illuminara**  
Twelve hours. Ten and a half. Nine and a bit. Each gap is seven-eighths of the one before it.

**Maren Vask**  
A decaying signal. Alarms do that. So does a fuse.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. And a fuse has an end. The last gap was four hours forty-three, and seven times that is thirty-three hours. At about one tomorrow afternoon the gaps are shorter than the pulses, and the pulses run together into one. Your Key turns two hours and twenty minutes before that.
Nobody on the deck said anything. One of the nine clocks ticked over, three seconds ahead of its neighbour.

**Illuminara**  
It is an ending or a beginning. I do not know which, and neither do you. Before anything else I want a way of finding out that none of us has to take on faith.

scenes.title: Seven-Eighths
paragraphs: *Operations hall, Kerrel's Anchor · Day one, 07:40*

The delegates came by relay. Commander Vask for Kerrel. Iyo-Seven for the Ussu Chorus, seven bodies in a tide-tank who spoke by turns. Tally for the Halcyon fleet, a point of cold light on the table that answered in the flat, courteous voice of a machine that had decided long ago not to be liked.
Illuminara set two stories side by side and asked them to distrust both equally.

**Illuminara**  
Story one: a being from outside our cosmos is in labour. The gaps shorten because that is what labour does, and between pulses the strain falls back to the same floor, because between contractions a body rests. Story two: an incursion wearing a mother's shape. The gaps shorten because the weapon is nearly ready, and between pulses the floor would climb, because a thing that is charging does not rest.

**Maren Vask**  
Story two is the one a mother's story is built to hide.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. So I am not asking you to believe either. I am asking you to predict. Each of you measures the pulses with your own instruments and seals when the next one begins and how high the floor sits after it. Nobody opens an envelope until the pulse has come.

**Tally**  
Kerrel keeps time by atoms, the Chorus by song, my fleet by ranging pulsars. Our errors are unrelated. If all three of us land together, it will not be because we copied one another.

**Iyo-Seven**  
Each pulse unmakes the songs of our young. We do not ask for pity. We ask that your test be quick.

The tenth pulse began at 08:07 and held the sky for forty minutes. Tally had sealed 08:06, the Chorus 08:09, Kerrel 08:05. Behind the swell the floor dropped back to where it had dropped before, within the width of a pencil line.

**Maren Vask**  
Once. A coin can land once.

**Illuminara**  
A coin can. So we throw it again at every pulse, and we write down now what would make us stop. If the floor rises more than three parts in a hundred of the peak, or a gap breaks the seven-eighths by more than a quarter of itself, the story is false and the Key turns. We write that while none of us is frightened. We will not be able to write it when we are.
Tally logged the line without comment. After a moment so did Iyo-Seven, seven bodies nodding out of step. Vask took longest.

**Maren Vask**  
And while the coin is in the air, you intend to go and ask the thing itself.

**Illuminara**  
I intend to ask it what no instrument of yours can read.

**Wren Odira**  
I keep the clock. I say your name every hour. You answer, or I come in.

**Illuminara**  
You can't come into a window.

**Wren Odira**  
Watch me find out.

scenes.title: The Window
paragraphs: *Tide-boat Long Patience, outer reach · Day one, 09:20*

The Long Patience hung a light-year and a half from the guest, as near as the Ussu would take her. Illuminara felt the thing out in the dark as a slow tilt in the floor of everything, a hill her body leaned away from.

She made the window the way she had made them before, a place where one consciousness could meet another without either being crushed. She knew its limits as she knew her own hands: it could be widened to take a weight far larger than she was, for a while, and past a certain width it stopped being a window and became something that broke the one holding it. The guest came into it as a long dim shoreline, warm at the far end, with something at the warm end turning over in its sleep.

**Anomei**  
You are small, and not afraid enough. Good. The others sent engines.

**Illuminara**  
I am Illuminara. Are you hurting my cluster on purpose?

**Anomei**  
I am hurting it by being. You are a room, and I was offered a closet. At the first door they closed a gate. At the second they sang me away. At the third they sent a fleet. I did not come for your stars. I came for what I carry.

**Illuminara**  
Tell me what you carry.

**Anomei**  
A child. In your word, which is a poor word for it: soon.

**Anomei**  
I will tell you what I have told no one, because you asked and did not aim. If I am refused a place, I will bear the child where I stand. Its first breath will pour my home's law into your space: a core that takes everything it holds, and a fringe felt three light-years across. It will not be malice. It will be a birth. I would rather be the thing you fear than watch my child die in a closet.
Illuminara did not soften it. She had learned long ago that the worst thing to do with a true threat was to make it smaller for the people who had to decide about it.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will carry that sentence to three suspicious powers exactly as you said it. They need to know what refusing you costs, and they will believe the rest only if you have hidden nothing. Anomei had no measure for it in any language Illuminara could translate. So she went to the stars.

Every star in the cluster had swung by an amount she could read, and every star had a known weight and distance. She laid the swings against the rule and asked what size of pressing thing would draw that curve. There is a void at the cluster's edge. Dornrath. Nothing in it larger than a comet for nearly two light-years in every direction.

**Anomei**

**Illuminara**  
It is not nobody's. Nine thousand people live on its rim, in the dark, on purpose. Asking them is the first thing I must do, and they can say no.

**Anomei**  
Then I must wait for an answer from strangers about my child. I have never asked a stranger for anything.

**Wren Odira**  
Illuminara.

**Illuminara**  
Here, Wren. Hour one. Here.

So you have come to rent our dark.

**Illuminara**

**Pell Auro**  
And if I do?

**Illuminara**

Then you ask nine thousand people to stake their lives on your arithmetic.

**Illuminara**

**Corin Daas**  
One point three, at the end of the series. Not a little under one.
His fit leaned hardest on the nearest star, the bright one the charts called Wick.

**Illuminara**

He did, with his lips moving.

**Corin Daas**  
Nought point nine seven.

**Illuminara**  
Then I was a little low and you were a good deal high, and the double was the whole difference. Use your figure, not mine.
Tally ran his corrected model back over the eleven pulses so far. It had called every swing to within two parts in a hundred, and she logged that figure beside his name.

**Pell Auro**

Illuminara laid the plan out for the Elder and, by relay, for Vask and Iyo-Seven. Only the end of the series could say whether this was a mother or a weapon, so the plan had to hold even if the worse story were true. The fleets would hold at three light-years, so that if the story broke they would strike in the middle of an empty ocean, with nothing of theirs or the Tenders' within reach.

**Maren Vask**  
The Key has a deadline. Ten-forty.

**Illuminara**  
It turns when the floor rises or a gap breaks, as we wrote this morning, and on nothing else.

**Maren Vask**  
Then it waits on your conditions. There will be no second warning.

**Pell Auro**  
Not enough. Your three powers hold three sealed envelopes. We will hold a fourth. Corin reads the core on our instruments at every hop, not Halcyon's. **Maren Vask**

**Illuminara**  
Yes. It is also the only hand that belongs to the people nearest the harm. I would rather have a veto I cannot talk past than a yes I bought.
Vask looked at the flat line on the wall for as long as Pell had.

**Maren Vask**

**Pell Auro**

**Maren Vask**  
Done.

**Pell Auro**

**Illuminara**  
I will tell her exactly that.

scenes.title: Five Windows
paragraphs: *The outer lanes · Day one, 15:33 to Day two, 01:30*

Hop one opened at 15:33, the instant the twelfth pulse released the sky. The officers on the Anchor's deck had stopped saying story two.
The fifteenth pulse came eleven minutes early.
It came at 21:56 where all three predictions had said 22:07, and the sky tilted and held. On the Anchor's deck Vask's hand went to the Key before the thought did.

It is early. It broke the series.

**Tally**

**Illuminara**

The hand stayed. That crisis was over, and had been paid for in advance. The other one was not.

The early pulse had shifted the series. **Anomei**

**Maren Vask**

Seven bodies in a tide-tank began to sing as one, for the first time in Illuminara's hearing.

**Maren Vask**

**Iyo-Seven**

Hop five opened at 00:42, and with the strain held steady along the line it took forty-one minutes. At 01:23 the guest unfolded at the heart of the Dornrath void with two minutes to spare, and the sky of the Reach, for the first time in four days, did not tilt.
